My work is in health economics, with a focus on insurance markets and the
regulatory machinery behind them. Three threads run through it.

## Insurer capital regulation

Health insurers hold capital against risk under the NAIC's risk-based capital
formula, and they can change what that formula requires of them — most directly
by ceding premium to a reinsurer. I am interested in what insurers pay for that
relief, what the price reveals about how binding the requirements are, and
whether the capital freed up is put to productive use.

## Coverage expansion and market design

The Affordable Care Act left states a good deal of discretion, and they have used
it differently: reinsurance waivers, mandate structures, and Medicaid
arrangements vary widely. These differences make useful variation for studying
how coverage, premiums, and insurer participation respond to policy design.

## Prices and transparency

Federal rules now require hospitals and insurers to publish negotiated prices.
The resulting data are large, messy, and inconsistently posted, but they describe
a part of the health system that was previously unobservable. I have worked on
assembling and standardizing these files, and I am interested in what they show
about how market structure affects what payers actually pay.
